einzeiler: Novelist Sarah Pearce discusses her dark tech thriller about a dating app for corpses
kurzfassung: Host Rachel Feltman interviews author Sarah Pearce about her debut novel For Human Use. The conversation explores how modern dating apps commodify romance and inspire bizarre cultural satires. They also discuss generational divides in technology use and the psychological drive for authentic human connection.
stichpunkte: Sarah Pearce wrote the debut novel For Human Use, featuring a fictional dating app that matches users with dead bodies.
The core concept emerged from a surreal dream the author had shortly after moving in with her husband.
The book satirizes the influx of tech startup culture and financing models into New York during the mid-2010s.
Pearce notes a generational divide in humor and app perception depending on whether readers remember September 11th.
Dating apps have shifted from tools for meeting people into endless loops of swiping without real-life interaction.
The author observes that modern dating culture pushes people toward a frictionless existence that ultimately hinders genuine bonds.
Despite the difficulties and demoralizing nature of modern dating, Pearce advises singles to keep trying.

clips.hook: Appreciating the book depends on your age
clips.text: Reader enjoyment relies heavily on whether someone was old enough to watch televised news during a major historical tragedy.

clips.hook: A corpse at the front door in a dream
clips.text: The writer envisioned a dead body waiting outside her apartment shortly after moving in with her romantic partner.

beschreibung:
What if a dating app could optimize human connection, even after death? In this episode of Science Quickly, books and culture editor Bri Kane speaks with author Sarah Pierce about her debut novel For Human Use, a darkly comic thriller centered on a dating app that matches users with dead bodies. Pierce discusses dating apps, human behavior and the search for meaningful connection. Together, they explore what modern dating technology can and can’t offer and what our reactions to a truly bizarre innovation reveal about human behavior.

Recommended Reading:
